nodes.name: Induction hypothesis for $k-2$
nodes.statement: Assume $\phi(\mathbf{d}_{k-2}) \subseteq \mathcal{G}_{k-2}^{k/2 -1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction hypothesis for $k-2$

nodes.name: Last two steps must be up then down
nodes.statement: In the case of $k$, the last two steps appended to $\mathbf{d}_{k-2}$ has to be $1$ followed by $-1$ in order for $\mathbf{d}_k$ to be a Dyck path.
nodes.statement_short: Last two steps must be up then down

nodes.name: The appended pair adds one leaf vertex
nodes.statement: By induction hypothesis, this generates a graph with one extra vertex from the parent node, whose walk traversed at the last two steps of the walk.
nodes.statement_short: The appended pair adds one leaf vertex

nodes.name: Apply $\psi$ then $\phi$ to a Dyck path
nodes.statement: Apply $\psi$ to a given Dyck path $\mathbf{d}$ by definition, then apply $\phi$ to get a new sequence $\mathbf{d}'$ such that $d_j' = 1$ for new vertex, $-1$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\psi$ then $\phi$ to a Dyck path

nodes.name: New vertices correspond to up steps
nodes.statement: For the original Dyck path, the new vertex is the up step corresponding to $1$.
nodes.statement_short: New vertices correspond to up steps

nodes.name: $\phi$ recovers the original path
nodes.statement: This implies $\phi$ recovers the original Dyck path.
nodes.statement_short: $\phi$ recovers the original path

nodes.name: Encode a binary tree by preorder traversal
nodes.statement: Given a binary tree with $k$ nodes, perform preorder traversal: for each internal node visited, write an up-step \(U = (1,1)\). For each time return from a child, write a down-step \(D = (1,-1)\).
nodes.statement_short: Encode a binary tree by preorder traversal

nodes.name: Equal numbers of up and down steps give a Dyck path
nodes.statement: Since every internal node has exactly two children, there are \(k/2\) \(U\)'s and \(k/2\) \(D\)'s, giving a Dyke path of length \(k\).
nodes.statement_short: Equal numbers of up and down steps give a Dyck path

nodes.name: Inverse map from Dyck paths to trees
nodes.statement: Conversely, given a Dyck path, $U$ is interpreted as adding new node while $D$ is returning to the parent node.
nodes.statement_short: Inverse map from Dyck paths to trees

nodes.name: Set up induction on $k$
nodes.statement: We proceed by induction on $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up induction on $k$

nodes.name: Base case $k=1$
nodes.statement: Our base case is $k=1$, then: $$ Y_n^1 = Y_n \quad \Rightarrow \quad [Y_n^1]_{ij} = Y_{ij}, $$ which matches the formula since the summation over zero indices just gives the term $Y_{ij}$.
nodes.statement_short: Base case $k=1$

nodes.name: Expand $Y^{k+1}=Y^kY$ using the hypothesis
nodes.statement: Our inductive step is to assume that the formula holds for some $k \ge 1$, i.e., $$ \left[Y_n^k\right]_{ij} = \sum_{1 \le i_2, \dots, i_k \le n} Y_{i i_2} Y_{i_2 i_3} \cdots Y_{i_k j}. $$ We must show that it holds for $k + 1$. Note that: \begin{align*} \left[Y_n^{k+1}\right]_{ij} &= \sum_{\ell = 1}^n \left[Y_n^k\right]_{i\ell} Y_{\ell j} \\ &= \sum_{\ell = 1}^n \left( \sum_{1 \le i_2, \dots, i_k \le n} Y_{i i_2} Y_{i_2 i_3} \cdots Y_{i_k \ell} \right) Y_{\ell j} \\ &= \sum_{1 \le i_2, \dots, i_k, i_{k+1} \le n} Y_{i i_2} Y_{i_2 i_3} \cdots Y_{i_k i_{k+1}} Y_{i_{k+1} j}. \end{align*} Thus, the formula holds for $k + 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $Y^{k+1}=Y^kY$ using the hypothesis

nodes.name: Conclude for all $k$
nodes.statement: By induction, the result holds for all $k \ge 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude for all $k$

nodes.name: Start from the product over walk edges
nodes.statement: Using lemma \ref{lem:multi_index_graph_equivalence}, we already have that $Y_{\mathbf{i}} = \prod_{w \in w_{\mathbf{i}}} Y_{w}$. We consider the following cases for each $(i, j)$:
nodes.statement_short: Start from the product over walk edges

nodes.name: Edge not on the walk contributes 1
nodes.statement: \textbf{$(i, j) \notin w_{\mathbf{i}}$}: In this case, the entry $Y_{ij}^{w_{\mathbf{i}}(\{i, j\})} = 1$, making no contribution to the product.
nodes.statement_short: Edge not on the walk contributes 1

nodes.name: Edge on the walk contributes its multiplicity
nodes.statement: \textbf{$(i, j) \in w_{\mathbf{i}}$}: In this case, the entry $Y_{ij}^{w_{\mathbf{i}}(\{i, j\})}$ is equal to the number of times the unordered edge $\{i, j\}$ appears in the path $w_{\mathbf{i}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Edge on the walk contributes its multiplicity

nodes.name: Combine the cases into the product formula
nodes.statement: These two cover all possibilities, so putting them together we obtain $$ Y_{\mathbf i} \;=\; \prod_{1\le i\le j\le n} Y_{ij}^{\,w_{\mathbf i}(\{i,j\})}. $$ Indeed, if $(i,j)\notin w_{\mathbf i}$ then $w_{\mathbf i}(\{i,j\})=0$ and the corresponding factor contributes $Y_{ij}^{0}=1$, and if $(i,j)\in w_{\mathbf i}$ (hence also $(j,i)$ if $j<i$), the exponent $w_{\mathbf i}(\{i,j\})$ counts exactly how many times the unordered edge $\{i,j\}$ appears in the walk, so the factor is $Y_{ij}^{\,w_{\mathbf i}(\{i,j\})}$. Because every unordered pair $\{i,j\}$ with $1\le i\le j\le n$ is covered by one of these two cases and the product lists each edge exactly once.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the cases into the product formula

nodes.name: Independence factorizes the expectation
nodes.statement: Because each $Y_{ij}$ is independent, we can write: $$ \bE(Y_{\mathbf{i}}) = \bE\left(\prod_{1 \leq i \leq j \leq n} Y_{ij}^{w_{\mathbf{i}}(\{i, j\})}\right) = \prod_{1 \leq i \leq j \leq n} \bE(Y_{ij}^{w_{\mathbf{i}}(\{i, j\})}) $$ using lemma \ref{lem:graph_walk_count_equivalence}. Consider the following cases for each $(i, j)$ (we assume each $(i, j) \in w_{\mathbf{i}}$ since if they aren't, then $w_{\mathbf{i}}(i, j) = 0$ and this contributes nothing to the product):
nodes.statement_short: Independence factorizes the expectation

nodes.name: Diagonal factors equal moments of $Y_{11}$
nodes.statement: $\mathbf{i = j}$: in this case, we have $Y_{ij} = Y_{ii}$, and therefore the edge $(i, i) \in E_{\mathbf{i}}^{s}$. Since each $Y_{ii}$ is identically distributed for all $i$, we have: $$ \bE(Y_{ii}) = \bE(Y_{11}) $$ so the factor in the product above becomes $\bE(Y_{ij}^{w_{\mathbf{i}}(\{i, j\})}) = \bE(Y_{11}^{w_{\mathbf{i}}(i, i)})$.
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal factors equal moments of $Y_{11}$

nodes.name: Off-diagonal factors equal moments of $Y_{12}$
nodes.statement: $\mathbf{i < j}$: in this case, we have $Y_{ij} \in E_{\mathbf{i}}^{c}$. Since each non diagonal entry $Y_{ij}$ is identically distributed for all $i \neq j$ (and by symmetry $Y_{ij} = Y_{ji}$), we have: $$ \bE(Y_{ij}) = \bE(Y_{12}) $$ so the factor in the product above becomes $\bE(Y_{ij}^{w_{\mathbf{i}}(\{i, j\})}) = \bE(Y_{12}^{w_{\mathbf{i}}(i, j)})$.
nodes.statement_short: Off-diagonal factors equal moments of $Y_{12}$

nodes.name: Combine both cases
nodes.statement: Plugging both of these cases into the earlier product over $E_{\mathbf{i}}^{c}$ and $E_{\mathbf{i}}^{s}$, we have: $$ \prod_{1 \leq i \leq j \leq n} \bE(Y_{ij}^{w_{\mathbf{i}}(\{i, j\})}) = \prod_{e_s \in E_{\mathbf{i}}^s} \bE(Y_{11}^{w_{\mathbf{i}}(e_s)}) \cdot \prod_{e_c \in E_{\mathbf{i}}^c} \bE(Y_{12}^{w_{\mathbf{i}}(e_c)}) $$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Combine both cases

nodes.name: Express $Y_\mathbf{j}$ via the permutation
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi$ be the permutation that maps $w_\mathbf{i}$ to $w_{\mathbf{j}}$ in the equivalence relation. Given $Y_\mathbf{i} = Y_{i_1 i_2}Y_{i_2 i_3} \cdots Y_{i_{k-1} i_k}Y_{i_k i_1}$, we have \[ Y_{\mathbf{j}} = Y_{j_1 j_2}Y_{j_2 j_3} \cdots Y_{j_{k-1} j_k}Y_{j_k j_1} = Y_{\varphi(i_1) \varphi(i_2)}Y_{\varphi(i_2) \varphi(i_3)} \cdots Y_{\varphi(i_{k-1}) \varphi(i_k)}Y_{\varphi(i_k) \varphi(i_1)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Express $Y_\mathbf{j}$ via the permutation

nodes.name: Permutation preserves loops
nodes.statement: Observe that $\{ i_{\lambda_l},i_{\lambda_{l+1}} \}$ is a singleton and only if $\{ \varphi(i_{\lambda_l}),\varphi(i_{\lambda_{l+1}}) \}$ is a singleton.
nodes.statement_short: Permutation preserves loops

nodes.name: Permutation preserves edge coincidences
nodes.statement: The fact that $\{ i_{\lambda_l},i_{\lambda_{l+1}} \} = \{ i_{\lambda_\mu},i_{\lambda_{\mu+1}} \}$ if and only if $\{ \varphi(i_{\lambda_l}),\varphi(i_{\lambda_{l+1}}) \} = \{ \varphi(i_{\lambda_\mu}),\varphi(i_{\lambda_{\mu+1}}) \}$ completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Permutation preserves edge coincidences

nodes.name: Take a class with a singly traversed edge
nodes.statement: Let $(G,w) \in \mathcal{G}_k$ and let $\mathbf{j}$ be the $k$-index generated by $(G,w)$. Suppose there exists an edge $e \in E_\mathbf{j}$ such that $w_\mathbf{j}(e) = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a class with a singly traversed edge

nodes.name: A factor $\bE(Y_{ij})$ appears in the product formula
nodes.statement: This means, in Lemma \ref{lem:expectation_matrix_multi_index}, a singleton term $\bE (Y_{ij}^{w_\mathbf{j}(e)}) = \bE (Y_{ij})$ appears.
nodes.statement_short: A factor $\bE(Y_{ij})$ appears in the product formula

nodes.name: Mean-zero entries make the product vanish
nodes.statement: The rest of the proof follows from the assumption of Proposition \ref{???} that $\bE (Y_{ij}) = 0$ for every $i$ and $j$.
nodes.statement_short: Mean-zero entries make the product vanish

nodes.name: Only the fraction depends on $n$
nodes.statement: The only part that depends on $n$ is the big fraction.
nodes.statement_short: Only the fraction depends on $n$

nodes.name: Vertex bound $|G_w|\le k/2+1$
nodes.statement: Since we only care about $w \ge 2$, $|G_w| \le k/2 + 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Vertex bound $|G_w|\le k/2+1$

nodes.name: Falling factorial asymptotic to power gives boundedness
nodes.statement: Use the fact that the product $n(n-1)\cdots (n-|G|+1)$ is asymptotically equal to $n^{|G|}$ to conclude that the fraction is bounded and doesn't explode.
nodes.statement_short: Falling factorial asymptotic to power gives boundedness

nodes.name: Author's note that the proof is outdated
nodes.statement: Proof slightly outdated.
nodes.statement_short: Author's note that the proof is outdated

nodes.name: Each edge traversed twice gives $k/2$ edges
nodes.statement: Let $(G,w)\in\mathcal{G}^{k/2+1}_k$. Since $w$ traverses each edge exactly twice, the number of edges in $G$ is $k/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Each edge traversed twice gives $k/2$ edges

nodes.name: Tree characterization gives a tree without self-edges
nodes.statement: Since the number of vertices is $k/2+1$, Exercise (Prop) 4.3.1 shows that $G$ is a tree. In particular there are no self-edges (as we saw already in Proposition 4.4).
nodes.statement_short: Tree characterization gives a tree without self-edges

nodes.name: Justify the four equalities of the chain
nodes.statement: 1st equality: definition right after equation 4.4 in notes 2nd equality: proposition 4.4 (w < 3) and previous lemma (w = 1 --> 0) 3nd equality: definition (from main proposition) 4th equality: number of edges is k/2.
nodes.statement_short: Justify the four equalities of the chain

nodes.name: Finitely many edges in the joined graph
nodes.statement: Let $(G_{\mathbf{i}\#\mathbf{j}},w_\mathbf{i},w_\mathbf{j})$ be the ordered triple generated by the two $k$-indexes $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$. By construction, there are finite number of edges $e \in E_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Finitely many edges in the joined graph

nodes.name: Finitely many multiplicity values
nodes.statement: Moreover, there are finite number of integer values the counting function $w_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}(\cdot)$ can take over $E_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Finitely many multiplicity values

nodes.name: Choose the maximal moment and its exponent
nodes.statement: This implies we can choose the maximum element of the set \[ \mathscr{E} := \{ \mathbb{E} (Y_{11}^\lambda) : \lambda = w_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}(e) \text{ for some } e \in E_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}} \}, \] and therefore $\lambda \in \mathbb{N}$ so that $\mathbb{E}(Y_{11}^\lambda) = \max \mathscr{E}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose the maximal moment and its exponent

nodes.name: Bound by $r_\lambda$
nodes.statement: Using the fact that $\mathbb{E}(Z) \leq \mathbb{E}(|Z|)$ for any random variable $Z$, \[ \mathbb{E} (Y_{11}^{w_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j} (e)}}) \leq \max\{ \mathbb{E}(|Y_{11}^\lambda|), \mathbb{E}(|Y_{12}^\lambda|) \} = r_\lambda. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound by $r_\lambda$

nodes.name: Edgewise factorization
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:expect_mul_eq_prod_expect_edgewise_of_indep}, we have \[ \mathbb{E} (Y_\mathbf{i}Y_\mathbf{j}) = \prod_{e_s \in E^s_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}} \mathbb{E} (Y_{11}^{w_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}(e_s)}) \cdot \prod_{e_c \in E^c_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}} \mathbb{E} (Y_{12}^{w_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}(e_c)}). \]
nodes.statement_short: Edgewise factorization

nodes.name: Bound diagonal factors
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:expect_pow_edge_count_pair_le}, there exists $\lambda_1 \in \mathbb{N}$ so that $\mathbb{E} (Y_{11}^{w_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j} (e)}}) \leq r_n$ for every $e \in E_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound diagonal factors

nodes.name: Bound off-diagonal factors
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by Lemma \ref{lem:expect_pow_edge_count_pair_le_off}, there exists $\lambda_2 \in \mathbb{N}$ so that $\mathbb{E} (Y_{12}^{w_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j} (e)}}) \leq r_m$ for every $e \in E_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound off-diagonal factors

nodes.name: Bound the product
nodes.statement: Then \[ \mathbb{E} (Y_\mathbf{i}Y_\mathbf{j}) = \prod_{e_s \in E^s_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}} \mathbb{E} (Y_{11}^{w_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}(e_s)}) \cdot \prod_{e_c \in E^c_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}} \mathbb{E} (Y_{12}^{w_{\mathbf{i} \# \mathbf{j}}(e_c)}) \leq 2k \cdot \max\{r_{\lambda_1},r_{\lambda_2}\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound the product

nodes.name: Define $M_1$
nodes.statement: Setting $M_1 := 2k \cdot \max\{r_{\lambda_1},r_{\lambda_2}\}$ satisfies the problem.
nodes.statement_short: Define $M_1$

nodes.name: Every edge of the joined graph is traversed
nodes.statement: By construction, every edge in the joined graph $G_{{i}\#{j}}$ is traversed at least once by the union of the two paths $w_{i}$ and $w_{j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Every edge of the joined graph is traversed

nodes.name: Consider an edge traversed once
nodes.statement: Suppose that $e$ is an edge that is traversed only {\em once}. This means that $w_{{i}\#{j}}(e) = 1$, and so it follows that the two values $w_{i}(e),w_{j}(e)$ are $\{0,1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Consider an edge traversed once

nodes.name: Mean-zero entries make $\pi$ vanish
nodes.statement: Hence, the above expansion and the fact that $\bE(Y_{11})=\bE(Y_{12})=0$ show that $\pi(G_{{i}\#{j}},w_{i},w_{j}) = 0$ in this case.
nodes.statement_short: Mean-zero entries make $\pi$ vanish

nodes.name: Limit bounded by $C_k$
nodes.statement: From proposition \ref{prop:matrix_moments_convergence}, we know that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}(\mathbf{X}_{n}^{k}) \leq C_{k}$ (odd and even cases of $k$).
nodes.statement_short: Limit bounded by $C_k$

nodes.name: Limsup equals the limit
nodes.statement: We further know that since the limit exists, $\lim \sup_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}(\mathbf{X}_{n}^{k}) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\operatorname{Tr}(\mathbf{X}_{n}^{k})$.
nodes.statement_short: Limsup equals the limit

nodes.name: Catalan bound $C_k\le 4^k$
nodes.statement: Using lemma \ref{lem:Catalan_bound}, we have: $$ \lim \sup_{n\to\infty }\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Tr}(\mathbf{X}_{n}^{k}) \leq C_{k} \leq 4^{k} $$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Catalan bound $C_k\le 4^k$

nodes.name: Sequence is nonnegative
nodes.statement: We know that for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lim\sup_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\int_{|x| > b}|x|^{k}\mu \mathbf{x}_{n}(dx)) \geq 0$ (lemma \ref{lem:nonnegative_sequence_lim_sup_p}).
nodes.statement_short: Sequence is nonnegative

nodes.name: Sequence bounded by a vanishing geometric term
nodes.statement: We also see that the sequence is bounded by $\frac{1}{\epsilon} (\frac{4}{b})^{k}$ (lemma \ref{lem:new_bound_for_lim_sup_p}), which is decreasing to $0$ as $k\to\infty$ (lemma \ref{lem:decreasing_sequence_1_over_epsilon_4_over_b_to_k}).
nodes.statement_short: Sequence bounded by a vanishing geometric term

nodes.name: Squeeze theorem
nodes.statement: Via squeeze theorem (where we use the zero sequence as another bound), we have: $$ \lim_{k\to\infty} \lim\sup_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\int_{|x| > b}|x|^{k}\mu \mathbf{x}_{n}(dx)) = 0 $$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Squeeze theorem

nodes.name: Define $a_k$ and invoke the zero criterion
nodes.statement: Consider sequence $(a_{k})_{k =1}^{\infty}$ defined as $a_{k} = \lim \sup_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\int_{|x| > b}|x|^{k} \mu\mathbf{x}_{n}(dx))$. Then, we use the conditions from lemma \ref{lem:all_terms_zero_conditions}:
nodes.statement_short: Define $a_k$ and invoke the zero criterion

nodes.name: Nonnegativity
nodes.statement: From lemma \ref{lem:nonnegative_sequence_lim_sup_p}, we know that $a_{k} \geq 0$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, so the sequence is nonnegative.
nodes.statement_short: Nonnegativity

nodes.name: Monotonicity
nodes.statement: From lemma \ref{lem:increasing_sequence_lim_sup_p}, we know that $a_{k+1} \geq a_{k}$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, so the sequence is strictly increasing.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity

nodes.name: Limit zero
nodes.statement: From lemma \ref{lem:limit_of_sequence_lim_sup_p}, we know that $\lim_{k\to\infty} a_{k} = 0$, so the sequence converges to zero.
nodes.statement_short: Limit zero

nodes.name: All terms vanish
nodes.statement: Therefore the sequence $a_{k} = \lim \sup_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(\int_{|x| > b}|x|^{k} \mu\mathbf{x}_{n}(dx)) = 0$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: All terms vanish
